What happened: Mediterranean storm Daniel flooded Greece, then caused catastrophic flooding in Libya, where dam failures devastated the coastal city of Derna.
Human impact: About 5,951+ deaths and 10,100+ missing; Greece damage about US$2.14 billion.

What happened: Atlantic storms that rapidly strengthen from Category 1 to major hurricane more than doubled between 1971–1990 and 2001–2020.

Event: State of the Climate report: 'uncharted territory'
What happened: A BioScience report signed by 15,000 scientists warned of systemic, existential climate threats.
Otis hit Acapulco as a Category 5, the strongest Pacific hurricane at landfall on record.
Human impact: 50–350 deaths (estimates vary); about US$16 billion damage.
Source 2 publisher: NOAA National Hurricane Center – Tropical Cyclone Report

What happened: 17 November 2023 was the first day the global average temperature was more than 2 °C above pre-industrial levels.

Event: Fossil fuel air pollution: 5.13 million excess deaths a year
What happened: About 5.13 million excess deaths a year were attributed to air pollution from fossil fuels.

Event: COP28: agreement to 'transition away' from fossil fuels
What happened: The 'UAE Consensus' called for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems and tripling renewable capacity by 2030, without a firm phase-out. The loss and damage fund was launched with about US$430m pledged.
Source 2 publisher: Wikipedia – 2023 United Nations Climate Change Conference

What happened: Fossil CO2 emissions were still rising; at current rates the 1.5 °C threshold could be exceeded around 2031.
Jasper became the wettest tropical cyclone in Australian history (2,252 mm).
Renewables generated 30% of global electricity in 2023.
Mass coral bleaching spread across all three ocean basins from early 2023, the start of the fourth global bleaching event (confirmed by NOAA in April 2024).

Event: 2023: hottest year on record (at the time)
What happened: 2023 was 1.48 °C above pre-industrial levels. Nearly half of all days were over 1.5 °C and two days exceeded 2 °C for the first time. CO2 averaged about 419.3 ppm.
The running 12-month global average temperature exceeded 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels for the first time.
Global sea surface temperatures set monthly records for 15 months in a row; March 2024 hit 21.07 °C, and 2024's annual average (20.87 °C) was the highest on record.

Event: First US commercial offshore wind farm powers up
What happened: Vineyard Wind began sending power to the grid from its first turbine (5 MW), with 62 turbines planned.
Wildfires swept into Viña del Mar and Quilpué; the deadliest fires in Chile's history and its worst disaster since the 2010 earthquake.

Event: Sea sponges suggest warming started earlier
What happened: Records preserved in long-lived Caribbean sea sponges suggest warming began in the 1860s and reached about 1.7 °C by 2020, 0.5 °C more than IPCC estimates.
Simulations found an early-warning signal that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation is on route to tipping.
Long-rains flooding hit East Africa.
Repeated heatwaves across North America through spring and summer.
Repeated flash floods hit Afghanistan and Pakistan.

Event: Melting ice is changing Earth's spin and day length
What happened: Melting polar ice has slowed Earth's rotation; days lengthened about 1.33 milliseconds per century in the 21st century and could reach 2.62 ms/century by 2100 under high emissions.

Event: European Court of Human Rights rules against Switzerland
What happened: In a case brought by about 2,000 older Swiss women (KlimaSeniorinnen), the court found Switzerland's climate inaction breached their human rights.

Event: NOAA confirms fourth global coral bleaching event
What happened: NOAA confirmed the world was in its fourth global coral bleaching event on record (previous ones: 1998, 2010, 2014–2017).

Event: Gulf floods: UAE's heaviest rain on record
What happened: Al Ain in the UAE recorded 254.8 mm in under 24 hours, the most since UAE records began in 1949.
Human impact: At least 46 deaths across the region (20 in Oman).

What happened: The worst floods in over 80 years: Guaíba Lake in Porto Alegre rose to 5.31 m, beating the 1941 record, and 431 of 497 municipalities were hit.
Human impact: 181 deaths (61 missing); 580,000+ displaced; about US$3.7bn reconstruction.

Event: G7 agrees to end unabated coal power by 2035
What happened: G7 countries agreed to phase out unabated coal power by 2035.
The Humboldt Glacier shrank so much it was reclassified as an ice field, making Venezuela the first modern country to lose all its glaciers.
A long, extreme heatwave hit Pakistan.

Event: Law of the Sea tribunal: greenhouse gases are marine pollution
Location: International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (Hamburg)
What happened: ITLOS advised that greenhouse gases absorbed by the ocean count as marine pollution, so states must monitor and reduce them.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites Inside Climate News.

Event: Climate change added 26 extra days of extreme heat
What happened: Human-caused warming added an average of 26 extra days of extreme heat worldwide over the previous 12 months.
Source 1 publisher: Climate Central / Red Cross / World Weather Attribution (via Wikipedia)

Event: Vermont passes first US Climate Superfund law
What happened: Vermont became the first US state to make fossil fuel companies pay for climate damages.

Location: West and Central Africa (Nigeria, Chad, Niger and others)
What happened: Severe seasonal floods hit much of West Africa.
Climate link (as stated by source): Scientists said global warming worsened the floods (Al Jazeera report).

Event: Brazil's worst drought on record; Amazon rivers at all-time lows
What happened: At least 59% of Brazil was in drought. The Rio Negro at Manaus fell to 12.66 m on 4 Oct 2024, its lowest since records began in 1902; Lake Tefé, where 200+ dolphins died in 2023, dried up. Bolivia had record fires.
Extreme heat during the Hajj pilgrimage led to mass casualties.
Beryl became the earliest Category 5 Atlantic hurricane on record and set a June rapid-intensification record.

Event: Earth's hottest day and record heat stress
What happened: On 10 July a record 44% of the globe had strong to extreme heat stress (feels-like 59.1 °C in Algeria). 22 July set the hottest global average day on record: 17.16 °C.
Extreme monsoon rain triggered landslides that swept away villages.

Location: Philippines, China (Hainan), Vietnam, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand
What happened: Yagi caused extensive damage across South-East Asia and southern China.

Location: Poland, Czechia, Austria, Romania, Slovakia, Hungary, Germany
What happened: Parts of Poland got nearly half a year's rain in three days; Jeseník in Czechia got nearly 500 mm.
Helene hit Florida and caused catastrophic flooding far inland across the south-eastern US and the Appalachians.
Human impact: 252 deaths (deadliest mainland US hurricane since Katrina); about US$78.7 billion damage.

Event: UK closes its last coal power station
What happened: The closure of Ratcliffe-on-Soar ended 142 years of coal power in the UK.
A record number of US states (48) had at least moderate drought somewhere, the most in Drought Monitor history.
Milton became one of the most intense hurricanes ever in the Gulf of Mexico (tying Rita, 2005) before hitting Florida.
Source 2 publisher: NOAA National Hurricane Center – Tropical Cyclone Report

What happened: A 'cold drop' (DANA) storm, formed as cold air moved over the warm Mediterranean, dumped torrential rain on eastern Spain; towns such as Paiporta were devastated.
Human impact: 224 deaths in Spain (216 in Valencia province); the worst flood disaster in Europe since 2021.

Event: Record-low sea ice at both poles
What happened: Antarctic sea ice set a record low for November, and Arctic sea ice had its lowest December extent on record.

Event: Ocean warming supercharged every 2024 Atlantic hurricane
What happened: A study found warmer oceans increased the wind speeds of all 11 Atlantic hurricanes of 2024 (to that date) by 9–28 mph.

Event: COP29 Baku: US$300bn climate finance goal
What happened: Developed countries agreed to provide US$300 billion a year by 2035 for developing nations (many wanted US$500bn+); rules for a UN carbon credit market were also agreed.
Source 2 publisher: Wikipedia – 2024 United Nations Climate Change Conference

Event: Three-quarters of land has become permanently drier
What happened: The UN desertification body found over 75% of Earth's land has become permanently drier; a quarter of people live in expanding drylands.
Very likely sea-level rise by 2100: 0.3–1.0 m with low emissions and 0.5–1.9 m with high emissions.
The strongest storm to hit Mayotte in at least 90 years (gust of 226 km/h) and the costliest South-West Indian Ocean cyclone on record.
Human impact: At least 173 deaths (41 missing); about US$3.9 billion damage.

Event: Biggest one-year CO2 jump on record
What happened: CO2 rose 3.5 ppm from 2023 to 2024, the largest single-year rise since measurements began in 1957. Copernicus put 2024 CO2 at about 422.1 ppm.
Notes: Primary source: WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin No. 21.

Event: World's rivers and glaciers under stress
What happened: Only one-third of the world's river basins had normal conditions in 2024, and all glacier regions lost ice for a third year running.
Source 1 publisher: WMO – State of Global Water Resources 2024

Event: 2024: hottest year on record and first above 1.5 °C
What happened: 2024 was 1.60 °C above pre-industrial (Copernicus; WMO consolidated estimate 1.55 °C), the first calendar year above 1.5 °C. Water vapour hit a record and Europe had its warmest year.
Source 2 publisher: WMO – State of the Global Climate 2025 (press release)

Event: Biggest coral bleaching event ever: 84% of reefs
What happened: Bleaching-level heat stress hit 83.7% of the world's coral reef area, beating the previous record of 68.2% (2014–2017). Bleaching was confirmed in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans.
Climate link (as stated by source): Driven by record ocean temperatures.
Notes: 84% experienced bleaching-level heat stress; not every reef in that area fully bleached (see Science Feedback).

What happened: A violent Atlantic windstorm hit Ireland and the UK with gusts of up to about 135 mph.

Event: Part of the Arctic now releases more CO2 than it absorbs
What happened: At least 30% of the Arctic-boreal region has become a net source of CO2.
The first-ever blizzard warnings were issued for coastal Louisiana and Texas; Grand Coteau got a Gulf Coast record 13.4 in (34 cm) of snow.

Event: Ocean surface warming has sped up four-fold
What happened: The rate of sea surface warming rose from 0.06 °C per decade (1985–89) to 0.27 °C per decade (2019–23).
Wind-driven fires burned through Pacific Palisades and the Eaton area; Eaton and Palisades became California's 2nd and 3rd most destructive wildfires.
Human impact: About 30–31 deaths in official counts (some studies estimate far higher); 17,000+ structures destroyed or damaged.
Notes: Death tolls vary widely between sources.

What happened: A February heatwave forced school closures in South Sudan.
Climate link (as stated by source): World Weather Attribution: at least 2 °C hotter and 10 times more likely because of climate change.

What happened: A study found that 2024 being the first year above 1.5 °C suggests the world has likely entered a 20-year period at that level.

Event: Arctic sea ice: lowest winter maximum on record
What happened: Arctic sea ice peaked at about 14.19 million km², the lowest annual maximum since records began in 1979.
Source 1 publisher: WMO – State of the Global Climate 2025 (press release)

Event: Giant iceberg A23a grounds and breaks up
What happened: A23a, the world's largest iceberg (about 3,500 km² in Jan 2025), broke free in 2020 after being grounded since 1986, spun in an ocean vortex, grounded near South Georgia in March 2025 and began breaking apart in warmer water. By March 2026 it was about 180 km².
The most active March tornado outbreak on record.
WMO reported 2022–2024 saw the largest three-year loss of glacier mass on record.
Spain had its hottest summer on record (+2.1 °C) and Britain its hottest since records began in 1884.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites AFP and Reuters.

What happened: Days with marine heatwaves have tripled since 1940, and their intensity has risen by about 1 °C.

Event: Earth's energy imbalance twice IPCC estimate
What happened: Earth's energy imbalance in 2023 was about twice the IPCC's best estimate: the planet is trapping heat faster than expected.

Event: Glacier collapse buries Swiss village of Blatten
What happened: A glacier collapse near the Bietschhorn sent ice and debris into the valley, burying about 90% of Blatten, including 130 houses and the church.
Human impact: 1 death; about 300 residents evacuated beforehand (19 May).

What happened: A devastating flood hit the town of Mokwa.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites the Nigerian Tribune.

Event: 4 billion people got 30+ extra days of extreme heat
What happened: Climate change gave about 4 billion people at least 30 extra days of extreme heat in a year and doubled extreme-heat days in 195 countries.
Source 1 publisher: World Weather Attribution / Climate Central / Red Cross Climate Centre

What happened: Another severe monsoon season brought deadly floods to Pakistan.
Monthly CO2 at Mauna Loa topped 430 ppm for the first time.
Flash flooding along the Guadalupe River devastated communities in the Texas Hill Country.

Event: World Court advisory opinion on climate change
Location: International Court of Justice, The Hague
What happened: The International Court of Justice unanimously advised that states have legal obligations regarding climate change.
A landslide of over 64 million m³ fell into an Alaskan fjord, sending a wave up to 481 m up the opposite slope. Scientists linked it to conditions created by glacier retreat.
A deadly landslide struck the Jebel Marra area of Sudan.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites Radio Dabanga; death toll uncertain.

Event: Gulf of Panama ocean upwelling fails
What happened: The seasonal upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water in the Gulf of Panama failed for the first time in over 40 years of records.
A Nature study found human-caused warming made 2010–2019 heatwaves about 200 times more likely than in pre-industrial times.
Morocco became the 60th country to ratify the High Seas Treaty, triggering its entry into force on 17 January 2026.
Climate Action Tracker downgraded the US from 'insufficient' to 'critically insufficient'.
The Potsdam Institute's Planetary Health Check found the ocean acidification planetary boundary has been breached for the first time.
Typhoons and heavy rain caused severe floods in northern Vietnam.

Event: Renewables overtake coal in world electricity
What happened: In the first half of 2025, renewables (34.3%) generated more of the world's electricity than coal (33.1%) for the first time.

Event: Coral reefs crossing a tipping point
What happened: The Global Tipping Points Report 2025 said warm-water coral reefs are crossing their thermal tipping point.

Event: Lancet: 2.5 million deaths from fossil fuel pollution
What happened: The Lancet estimated 2.52 million deaths in 2022 from air pollution caused by burning fossil fuels.

Melissa made landfall in Jamaica on 28 Oct as a Category 5 with about 185 mph winds: the strongest hurricane ever to hit Jamaica, tying the Atlantic records for strongest landfall and strongest sustained winds.
Human impact: 95 deaths (Jamaica 45, Haiti 43); over US$12.2 billion damage in Jamaica, its costliest disaster.

What happened: Kalmaegi brought deadly flooding to the Philippines and Vietnam.
Days after Kalmaegi, Fung-wong brought extreme flooding and wind damage to the northern Philippines.
Scientists estimated the remaining carbon budget for 1.5 °C is about four years of current emissions.

Event: Turkey to host COP31 with Australia leading talks
What happened: After a standoff, Turkey won the right to host COP31 in Antalya, with Australia's climate minister Chris Bowen as 'President of Negotiations'.

The deal aims to triple adaptation finance by 2035 but has no explicit fossil fuel phase-out; voluntary roadmaps were announced outside the UN text. Brazil launched the US$125bn Tropical Forest Forever Facility. No high-level US delegation attended.

What happened: Ditwah struck Sri Lanka and southern India.
Only the second documented cyclone in the Strait of Malacca.
The Lancet Countdown found heat-related deaths averaged 546,000 a year in 2012–2021, up 63% from the 1990s.

Event: Caribbean reefs lost half their coral
What happened: Caribbean hard coral cover fell 48% between 1980 and 2024 as reef sea temperatures rose 1.07 °C (1985–2024).
A provisional EU deal set a target to cut greenhouse gases 90% by 2040 compared with 1990.

Event: 2025: second or third warmest year; 2015–2025 the 11 hottest
What happened: 2025 was about 1.43 °C above pre-industrial. Ocean heat hit a record for the ninth year running, sea level was about 11 cm above 1993, about 90% of the ocean surface had at least one marine heatwave, and Earth's energy imbalance reached a new high.
Source 1 publisher: WMO – State of the Global Climate 2025 (press release)
Source 2 publisher: WMO – State of the Global Climate 2025

Location: Victoria, New South Wales, South Australia
What happened: The most severe heatwave since 2019 hit Melbourne and Sydney; bushfires in Victoria burned 300,000+ ha. On 29–30 Jan Andamooka and Port Augusta reached 50 °C, with 12 sites above 49 °C.
Notes: Wikipedia entries cite The Guardian, PreventionWeb and Weatherzone. 2026 figures may be revised.

Event: Richest 1% use their yearly carbon budget in 10 days
What happened: Oxfam calculated the richest 1% used up their fair share of the annual carbon budget in just 10 days.
More than 150 million hectares burned worldwide in January–April 2026, 20% above the previous record.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites Reuters. 2026 figures may be revised.

Event: US announces exit from UN climate bodies
What happened: The US announced it would withdraw from the UNFCCC, the IPCC, the Green Climate Fund and dozens of other international organisations.
Notes: Wikipedia entries cite The New York Times and Politico. 2026 figures may be revised.

Event: Ocean heat record for ninth straight year
What happened: Ocean heat content reached a new record for the ninth year in a row (2025).
Wildfires burned through central-southern Chile.

Event: High Seas Treaty enters into force
What happened: The legally binding treaty to protect marine life in international waters came into force, allowing new marine protected areas on the high seas.

Event: Wind and solar overtake fossil power in the EU
What happened: Wind and solar supplied 30% of EU electricity in 2025, more than fossil fuels (29%), and beat fossil power in 14 of 27 countries.
Heavy rains caused deadly floods in Mozambique and Zimbabwe.
A major winter storm and deep freeze hit much of North America.
Source 1 publisher: Wikipedia – January 23–27, 2026 North American winter storm

Event: US completes second Paris Agreement exit
What happened: The United States' second withdrawal from the Paris Agreement took effect.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites The New York Times. 2026 figures may be revised.

Event: Dutch court rules for Bonaire islanders
What happened: The Hague District Court ruled the Dutch government discriminated against residents of the Caribbean island of Bonaire and ordered binding emissions targets and an adaptation plan.

Event: US EPA scraps the Endangerment Finding
What happened: The EPA formally rescinded its 2009 finding that greenhouse gases endanger public health, the legal basis for US climate rules. 24 states challenged it in court on 19 March.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites The Washington Post. 2026 figures may be revised.

Event: NOAA changes how it measures El Niño
What happened: NOAA adopted the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), which removes the effect of overall ocean warming when measuring El Niño and La Niña.

Event: Fish populations shrinking in warming waters
What happened: Fish biomass fell by up to 19.8% (1993–2021) in major Northern Hemisphere ocean regions.

Event: Record March heat in the US West
What happened: The contiguous US had its warmest March on record (+5.2 °C); Buttercup and Squaw Lake, California hit 112 °F, a US March record.
Notes: Wikipedia entries cite WWA, NCEI and Yale Climate Connections. 2026 figures may be revised.

What happened: A study found global warming sped up over 2015–2025, with more than 98% confidence.
Long-rains flooding hit Kenya again.
Floods and landslides hit Juiz de Fora, which had its wettest month on record.
Kona low storms dumped up to 1,395 mm of rain on Maui.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites NWS Honolulu. 2026 figures may be revised.

What happened: NOAA issued its final La Niña advisory as the Pacific moved to neutral conditions.

Event: New evidence the AMOC is weakening
What happened: Studies found the Atlantic overturning circulation weakened at four latitudes over 20 years, and estimated a future slowdown of 51±8%, stronger than most models predict.

Event: Mosquitoes found in Iceland for the first time
What happened: Mosquitoes were recorded in Iceland for the first time (in 2025), one of the last mosquito-free places.
In 2025, clean power growth exceeded electricity demand growth and renewables overtook coal.

Event: Southern Ocean may lock into low sea ice
What happened: A study suggested Antarctic sea ice may be shifting into a prolonged low state.

Event: UN General Assembly welcomes ICJ climate opinion
What happened: The UN General Assembly welcomed the ICJ's unanimous 2025 advisory opinion on states' climate obligations.
Violent storms swept across Uttar Pradesh.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites Le Monde. 2026 figures may be revised.

What happened: Kew reached 35.1 °C, an all-time May record, during a western European heat dome.

Event: WMO: 75% chance next 5 years average above 1.5 °C
What happened: WMO forecast annual temperatures of 1.3–1.9 °C above pre-industrial for 2026–2030, with a 75% chance the five-year average exceeds 1.5 °C.
Antarctica saw temperatures about 20 °C above normal in mid-winter, with ice thaw and rain on glaciers.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites Business Today. 2026 figures may be revised.

Event: UK sets 87% emissions cut target for 2040
What happened: The UK set a target to cut emissions about 87% by 2040 compared with 1990.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites Reuters. 2026 figures may be revised.

What happened: The EU announced a €92 million (about US$107m) ocean-monitoring project.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites AP News. 2026 figures may be revised.

What happened: The UN published its third World Ocean Assessment of the state of the marine environment.

Event: Extreme coastal floods 12 times more frequent
What happened: 1-in-100-year coastal floods have become about 12 times more frequent since 1900, and human-caused climate change has quadrupled their likelihood.
WMO confirmed El Niño had returned; on 11 June NOAA said El Niño conditions were present and expected to strengthen into winter 2026–27.

Event: UNICEF: nearly every child exposed to climate hazards
What happened: Almost all children face at least one climate hazard: 1.8 billion are exposed to droughts, 1.5 billion to heatwaves and 337 million to river floods.

Event: US moves to dismantle ocean observatory network
What happened: The US announced it would dismantle the Ocean Observatories Initiative (900 instruments); the move was paused on 18 June.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites The New York Times. 2026 figures may be revised.

What happened: Mid-year UN talks produced few tangible outcomes amid gridlock, though a package on a 'just transition mechanism' was agreed for COP31.
Châteaumeillant in France hit 43.3 °C as June records fell across western Europe.

What happened: Maysak brought floods to Vietnam and China; more than 130,000 people were evacuated.

Event: Drought declared across half of England
What happened: About 51.4% of England was in drought status.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites the Environment Agency. 2026 figures may be revised.

Event: August 2026: joint hottest month ever recorded
What happened: August 2026 averaged 16.96 °C, 1.65 °C above pre-industrial, tying July 2023 as the hottest month on record and the first month above 1.5 °C since November 2025. June–August was the joint-warmest on record, and western Europe had its hottest summer, beating 2003.
Yangsan reached 42.5 °C, a new national record.

Event: Hottest day ever recorded for the world's seas
What happened: 22 August 2026 set a record for the hottest day measured in the world's seas (about 21.10 °C daily average); August tied the all-time monthly sea-surface record.
A rock-and-ice avalanche from the Lirung massif near Langtang turned into a fast debris flow and flash flood down the Trishuli River, destroying the Gyirong border port area.

Event: Greenland and Antarctica lost 11,309 billion tonnes of ice
What happened: The two ice sheets lost about 11,309 gigatonnes of ice between 1979 and 2023, mostly from glaciers flowing faster into the sea.
Notes: Wikipedia entry cites Scientific Data. 2026 figures may be revised.

What happened: The Potsdam Institute found 7 of 9 planetary boundaries have been transgressed.

What happened: UN member states adopted a declaration on sea-level rise, a key demand of low-lying island nations.

A deep depression from the Bay of Bengal brought deadly floods.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 hurricane on 10 October.
A study estimated Thwaites Glacier will add about 30±6 mm to sea level by 2100.

What happened: The annual State of the Climate report in BioScience found 7 of 16 planetary vital signs at record extremes.

Imperial College London estimated about 50,391 heat deaths across 854 European cities, about two-thirds attributable to climate change.

Event: Latest start to an Atlantic hurricane season on record
What happened: The Atlantic had no hurricanes until after 10 September, the latest start since satellites began in the 1960s (El Niño tends to suppress Atlantic hurricanes).
